About this guidance

This guidance tells you how to carry out fair and effective asylum interviews to obtain relevant information to establish, as far as possible, whether the claimant meets the requirements for an asylum or human rights claim to succeed. It applies to any member of staff conducting an asylum interview for the purposes of gathering more information and evidence about the individual’s asylum claim. For further information about the screening interview see Asylum Screening and Routing guidance.

It provides specific guidance on:

interview arrangements and formalities

preparing for an asylum interview

how to investigate an asylum and human rights claim, including important principles, questioning techniques and factors that may affect an individual’s ability to provide evidence.

This instruction must be read alongside the main asylum policy instructions, on considering protection needs in asylum claims. In particular:

Assessing credibility and refugee status (select the version that relates to the date of the claim)

Asylum decision-making prioritisation

Certification under section 94 and 96

Dependants and former dependants

Disclosure and confidentiality of information in asylum claims

Family asylum claims

Gender identity issues in the asylum claim

Gender issues in the asylum claim

Medical evidence in asylum claims

Processing children’s asylum claims

Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim

Streamlined asylum processing

Withdrawing asylum claims

You must also refer to the relevant country policy and information notes, which include guidance on individual countries of origin. You may also wish to refer to the UNHCR’s Protection Handbook.

Contacts

If you have any questions about the guidance and your line manager or senior caseworker cannot help you or you think that the guidance has factual errors then email Asylum Policy Secretariat.

If you notice any formatting errors in this guidance (broken links, spelling mistakes and so on) or have any comments about the layout or navigability of the guidance then you can email the Guidance Review, Atlas and Forms team.

Purpose of guidance

Background

This guidance applies to anyone being interviewed in connection with their asylum application; an asylum applicant (or for the purposes of this guidance a ‘claimant’) being defined in Paragraph 327 of the Immigration Rules as a person who makes a request to be recognised as a refugee under the Refugee Convention or otherwise makes a request for international protection.

The asylum interview is an important part of the asylum process for many claimants because it is one of the main opportunities for the claimant to provide relevant evidence about why they need international protection and for you, as the person conducting the interview, to help draw out and test that evidence.

It is important that you create an environment in which claimants feel at ease and able to disclose all relevant information to you, allowing you to fully investigate the key issues through focused, professional and sensitive questioning. This is particularly relevant as some evidence may be highly complex and emotive, relating for example to instances of persecution or serious harm, including sexual violence or torture. Such evidence is crucial to ensure that asylum claims are properly considered, so that protection is granted to those who genuinely need it and refused to those who do not.

It is also important to remember that, in some circumstances and particularly in relation to highly sensitive information, disclosure may not happen during the interview, despite the interviewer’s best efforts. Claimants may be more comfortable disclosing sensitive information to immigration advisers, clinicians or support workers. Because of the sensitive information they need to share, they may elect to specify the sex of their interviewing officer and or interpreter in advance, or to highlight vulnerabilities and request the interview be omitted.

You should consider all information provided by the claimant in the round. Where a claimant fails to disclose information during an interview, this may impact their credibility adversely. But this is not an automatic finding, as there might be mitigating or compelling circumstances which you might need to consider.

Policy objective

The policy objective when you conduct an asylum interview is to gather enough evidence to be able to fairly and properly consider and determine the claim. You must:

provide a positive and secure environment to support the claimant to disclose all evidence, including sensitive information to support their claim

ensure that all asylum claimants are treated with respect, dignity and fairness regardless of their:

age

disability

ethnicity

nationality

race

gender

sexual orientation

religion or belief

ask appropriate, open and focused questions to encourage full disclosure and gather relevant evidence on important aspects of the claim – this will allow you to:

create an environment in which the claimant is able to present their case as fully as possible, to enable you to ascertain and evaluate the information they provide

assess the credibility of the claimant’s statements

give the claimant an opportunity to explain anything that appears to be implausible or inconsistent

identify any vulnerable claimants and safeguarding issues and make the relevant referrals to the Safeguarding Hub to enable signposting to appropriate support services for example, where there are concerns over physical and mental health, the claimant has experienced torture, sexual or domestic violence, or modern slavery, or there are child protection concerns

Asylum interviews: best interests of the child

Section 55 of the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009 requires the Home Office to carry out its functions in a way that takes into account the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children in the UK. In dealing with parents and children, you must see the family both as a unit and as individuals. Although a child’s best interests are not a factor in assessing whether a fear of persecution is well-founded, the way that you interact with children throughout the interview and the decision-making process, and any decisions following the determination of refugee status must take account of the section 55 duty.

You must comply with this duty when carrying out actions set out in this instruction in respect of children and those with children. You must follow the principles set out in the statutory guidance Every Child Matters - Change for Children.

Our statutory duty to children means you must demonstrate:

fair treatment which meets the same standard a British child would receive

the child’s best interests being a primary, although not the only, consideration

no discrimination of any kind

timely processing of asylum claims

identification of those who might be at risk from harm

Considering claims from those who are under eighteen must be conducted by decision-makers who have completed the requisite training and are qualified to interview and decide them. See Processing children’s asylum claims.

Even if a separate claim is not being made, it is important not to lose sight of the child as an individual, as well as part of a family, to be vigilant and responsive to their protection and welfare needs and to consider how this could impact on the needs of the family as a whole.

On 19 March 2021 the UK Supreme Court in G (Appellant) v G (Respondent) [2021]

UKSC 9 found that a child who is named as a dependant on an asylum claim can and should (generally) be understood to have made a claim for asylum in their own right. This means that child dependants must be treated as asylum claimants unless they do not have protection needs.

When a child is included as a dependant on an asylum claim, the main claimant is asked to explain whether that child has protection needs, and if they do, whether these are the same as, or additional or different to why the main claimant is claiming asylum.

Where a child has the same protection needs as that of the main claimant (their parent), they are considered to be an asylum claimant in their own right, but their asylum claim can be considered as part of a Family Asylum Claim. This means that the asylum claims of the main claimant and any dependent children with the same protection needs will be decided within a single consideration, using evidence provided by the main claimant. For further information, see the Family Asylum Claims guidance.

Where a child has additional or different protection needs to that of the main claimant, they are considered to be an asylum claimant in their own right, but their asylum claim cannot be considered as part of a Family Asylum Claim. Nor can the child be treated as a dependant on the asylum claim of the main claimant (their parent). The child’s claim must be considered as that of an accompanied asylum-seeking child, in accordance with the guidance on Processing children’s asylum claims.

Where a child does not have protection needs, they may continue to be treated as a dependant on the asylum claim of the main claimant.

There may be occasions where at the time of the asylum interview, it is unclear whether a dependent child has protection needs of their own. Where this is the case, you must ask the main claimant whether the child has protection needs and if so, whether they are the same as, additional or different to why they themselves are claiming asylum. Refer to the Family Asylum Claims guidance for detailed instructions on how to establish a child’s protection needs during a main claimant’s asylum interview.

You must keep the Section 55 duty in mind throughout the asylum interview and refer to other relevant guidance when necessary, including:

Dependants and former dependants

Processing children’s asylum claims

Family asylum claims

Safeguarding

Protecting vulnerable adults and children is a key cross-cutting departmental priority and safeguarding is everyone’s responsibility. If you become concerned that a claimant or dependant may be in danger at the interview or any other stage of the asylum process, you need to take immediate action to ensure their safety. In all circumstances a referral must be made to the relevant Safeguarding Hub and advice sought on case progression.

In an emergency, the case must be referred to emergency services without delay. The first person to become aware of an emergency, or where there is an immediate threat to life, must contact 999 and request the appropriate emergency service. Afterwards, you must then make a referral to the relevant Safeguarding Hub for actions to be progressed.

Safeguarding children

You must be vigilant that a child may be at risk of harm and where you are concerned about their welfare or protection issues, refer cases immediately (whether that child is a dependant of the asylum claim or not). In such circumstances you must immediately speak to the Safeguarding Hub, who will refer the case to the relevant local authority in accordance with the guidance in local authority child referrals. In an emergency, you must refer the case to emergency services immediately.

When referring cases involving children, there is no requirement to obtain the consent of any adults involved as the safeguarding of children is our primary responsibility as detailed in Section 55 of the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009.

The Safeguarding Advice and Children’s Champion (SACC) can also offer specialist safeguarding and welfare advice on issues relating to children, including family court proceedings and complex child protection cases. For more information see SACCSACC.

Signposting to support services

Asylum claimants receive the information booklet for asylum applications which includes information on support services and you can refer claimants to the contacts for appropriate support which are detailed in this leaflet.

Relevant legislation

Current UK asylum law is derived from a range of sources; international and European Law, primary and secondary legislation, the Immigration Rules (which are in turn supported by policy and guidance), and a substantial body of caselaw.

The 1951 Refugee Convention

The Refugee Convention is the primary source of international refugee protection. It has since been supplemented by the progressive development of international refugee and human rights law.

Under Paragraph 328 of the Immigration Rules, all asylum applications have to be decided in accordance with the Refugee Convention. Many of the principles set out in the Refugee Convention have been applied and interpreted by UK law, through statute, caselaw, immigration rules and policies.

The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)

The ECHR (formally the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms) is an international convention to protect human rights and political freedoms in Europe. Drafted in 1950 by the Council of Europe, the Convention entered into force on 3 September 1953. The Convention established the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). Any person who feels his or her rights have been violated under the Convention by a state party can take a case to the Court if they have exhausted all the domestic legal remedies available to him or her, if they have suffered a significant disadvantage and if the application is made within four months of the final domestic judicial decision.

The ECHR has been given effect to in UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998. This makes it unlawful for a public authority to act in breach of the UK’s obligations under the ECHR. Decision-makers are in some cases required to assess whether an individual has protection needs related to their rights under the ECHR and this is dealt with through separate guidance on claims for Humanitarian Protection and Family and Private Life.

European legislation

The EU set up the Common European Asylum System (CEAS), consisting of a series of legislative measures at an EU level, which introduced minimum and then common standards in the field of asylum. When a member of the EU, the UK opted into a number of the Directives within the CEAS with the obligations of those Directives being incorporated in UK legislation. The EU Directives themselves are no longer binding; however, any requirements that have been incorporated into UK legislation must continue to be complied with unless changed.

The Asylum (Procedures) Regulations 2007 together with the Immigration Rules transposed into UK law, Council Directive 2005/85/EC (the Procedures Directive). The Procedures Directive articles most relevant to this instruction are Articles 12 to 14 which specifically refer to asylum interviews and set out the requirements before a decision is taken on an asylum claim, including circumstances in which an interview can be omitted and when an interview may be recorded.

Nationality and Borders Act 2022

The Nationality and Borders Act 2022 (the 2022 Act) made changes to the way in which asylum claims made after 28 June 2022 are determined. The asylum interview guidance is relevant to all asylum claims, irrespective of the date that they were made.

The Immigration Rules

Part 11 of the Immigration Rules sets out the provisions for the consideration of asylum claims.

Paragraphs 339NA to 339ND of the Immigration Rules set out the basic provisions for asylum interviews and reflect our international obligations. These rules set out provisions for you to conduct an asylum interview, the circumstances when you can decide not to interview, a requirement that you treat evidence provided during an interview with appropriate confidentiality, and the provision of an interpreter during the interview.

Paragraph 339NC of the Immigration Rules sets out that a written report needs to be made of every interview and that the claimant should have timely access to the report to allow for any appeal.

Paragraph 339NE of the Immigration Rules introduced in the Statement of changes to the Immigration Rules: HC667 3 November 2016, sets out when you must make an audio recording of the personal interview and applies to all interviews conducted on or after 24 November 2016. See interview recording policy. Asylum interviews are audio recorded in line with articles 9(2)(f) and 9(2)(g) GDPR.

Paragraph 333C of the Immigration Rules enables you to treat a claim as withdrawn if the claimant fails to maintain contact with the Home Office and absconds prior to their asylum interview or fails to attend the interview without providing evidence that this was due to circumstances beyond their control. See Withdrawing asylum claims.

Paragraphs 339HA to 339N of the Immigration Rules are also relevant to the asylum interview because these set out the legal framework for considering the asylum claim, including that you must consider all the evidence provided by the claimant, including oral evidence provided at interview.

Sections 80B and 80C of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 set out, for asylum claims made on after 28 June 2022, the circumstances in which an asylum claim may be treated as inadmissible on safe third country grounds (for claims made before that date, paragraphs 345A-D of the Immigration Rules applied in a similar way). This is relevant because a person’s claim may be treated as inadmissible if before claiming asylum in the UK, they were present in, or had a connection to, a safe third country where they were safe and had or could have obtained protection. In some cases, this information may only come to light during the asylum interview. See inadmissibility on safe third country grounds.

The Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002

Section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002

Section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 allows you to certify a protection or human rights claim as clearly unfounded in line with the legislation and guidance. In all cases where a protection and or human rights claim falls to be refused, decision-makers must consider whether section 94 certification is appropriate and claims that are clearly unfounded should be certified unless an exception applies.

This is relevant because you must ensure relevant questions are asked during the interview to determine the appropriateness of certifying a claim. You must also be aware of the list of designated states whilst conducting asylum interviews. See the guidance on Certification of protection and human rights claims under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 (clearly unfounded claims).

The Nationality and Borders Act 2022 removed the out of country right of appeal for any claims certified under section 94 on or after 28 June 2022. This means that these cases no longer have a right of appeal against the decision. This applies irrespective of the date that the asylum and any human rights claim was made, so even if the claim was made on or before 27 June 2022, there will be no right of appeal if the claim is certified under section 94.

For further information on certification under section 94, see the guidance on Certification of protection and human rights claims under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 (clearly unfounded claims).

Section 94 trained decision makers

Asylum decision-makers who are signed off to conduct interviews and make decisions on asylum claims from adult claimants, and who have undertaken the dedicated section 94 training, can conduct asylum interviews with claimants entitled to reside in the countries listed in section 94(4) of the 2002 Act.

Decision Makers cannot interview claimants entitled to reside in countries listed in section 94(4) of the 2002 Act unless they have received the relevant section 94 training.

Section 96 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002

Section 96 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 allows you to certify a protection or human rights claim that could have been made earlier. Section 96 is intended to prevent claimants raising matters at the last minute to frustrate removal.

A claim can be certified under section 96 (if the conditions are met to do so) regardless of whether the right of appeal notified, or the section 120 notice served, was under the 2002 Act before its amendment by the Immigration Act 2014 or after its amendment.

You must not consider certification of a late claim under section 96 until you have considered the substantive merits of the claim and decided to refuse it. This is the case even where the claimant was shown to have lied or given an incomplete version of their story at their first appeal. For further information on certification under section 96, see the guidance on Late claims: certification under section 96 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Other legislation

Under Section 8 of the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.,) Act 2004, you must consider certain behaviours when assessing general credibility. You must provide the claimant with an opportunity to explain the reasons for such behaviour during the interview. See Section 8 for more information.

Interview arrangements

This section tells you how to arrange and conduct interviews and the behaviours expected of you as a representative of the Home Office when conducting an asylum interview.

Interview locations

Asylum interviews can be conducted in-person or remotely.

In-person (also referred to as face-to-face) interviews involve the interviewing officer and the claimant being in the same interview room as each other. In-person asylum interviews are conducted at Home Office locations around the UK, or at other secure and suitable locations such as HMPO buildings or large sites housing claimants.

Remote interviews are conducted via video conference (VC), which means that the claimant will not usually be in the same room as the interviewing officer. The claimant will be invited to a Home Office or Visas Facilitation Services (VFS) building, or another secure and suitable location for a remote interview, and the interviewing officer will be in a suitably private and quiet location.

Claimants will be advised in the invitation to interview whether their interview will be carried out in-person or remotely. Where a claimant has a reason why their interview should not be carried out by the method they have been allocated, they must let the Home Office know as soon as possible. It may take longer to schedule the asylum interview, but it will not impact the asylum decision.

There is also a remote asylum interviewing pilot taking place. For further information on the remote asylum interviewing pilot, refer to Remote video conferencing pilot

Personal conduct

In all interviews, irrespective of whether they are carried out in-person or remotely, you represent the Home Office and are expected to maintain high professional standards and treat claimants with dignity, respect, and sensitivity throughout. You must not wear overly casual or inappropriate clothing. You need to be aware of the impact your verbal and non-verbal communication may have on a claimant. Your body language should be open and relaxed and non-threatening, for example, keeping your arms uncrossed, and smiling where appropriate. This will help you to create an environment in which the claimant feels able to disclose relevant and potentially highly personal and sensitive information.

If the interview is to be carried out remotely by Video Conference (VC), you must conduct it from a suitably quiet and private area and be mindful of what the other attendees will be able to see and hear in the background. The standard of dress referred to above continues to apply to interviews conducted by VC. VC interviews can sometimes lose some of the key cues of communication that we all sub-consciously rely on, so it is important to make it clear at the start that you will be taking notes during the interview and will not always be able to look at the camera. You should also make time to look at the claimant regularly and make eye contact and nod and smile when appropriate.

Mobile phones

In order to avoid interruptions, and to ensure a confidential environment as far as possible, mobile phones must either be turned off during the interview or on silent (where possible). Mobile phones must not be used during the interview by either the interviewer, interpreter or the claimant, unless it is to make or answer an urgent call (for example, emergency calls, issues relating to children not present). The person receiving or making the call must request a break. Where a break is taken, the audio recording must be stopped and the reason for the break recorded on the interview transcript. The interview may need to be rescheduled if there is an urgent matter to deal with.

Invitation to interview

Unless one of the exceptions in paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules applies, you must invite claimants to attend an asylum interview using the relevant invitation to interview template adapted to include specific details for the date, time and location of the interview and whether the interview will take place in person or by VC at a location deemed appropriate.

You should endeavour to send an invitation to interview at least 7 days in advance of the interview taking place. The invitation to interview will state the scheduled duration of the interview. You must send a copy of the invitation to interview to the claimant and their immigration adviser, if there is one on record. See section on immigration advisers.

Interview appointments will usually be scheduled for 2-3 hours, although the interview may be longer or shorter in length. If further information needs to be gathered in order to decide a claim, then a follow up interview may be scheduled.

If the claimant, or their immigration adviser, considers that remote interviewing would not be suitable for them, they must contact the Home Office using the details provided in the invitation to interview, and provide reasons why it is not suitable in their case. You may also consider that an individual is not suitable to be interviewed by VC, and you can decide to invite them to an in-person interview instead. See appropriateness of interviewing by video conference.

Where paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules does not apply, the asylum interview is an important stage in the process and should not be cancelled or postponed without good reason. If the interview is postponed it should be rescheduled at the earliest opportunity. If the claimant requests a further delay, for example, to obtain a medical report detailing why they are unfit to be interviewed, this request should be considered in line with the section on non-attendance due to illness.

If the medical report does not pertain to fitness to interview, the request should explain, in brief, why it is necessary to delay the interview to await the medical report. It is unlikely that an interview should be delayed for a medical report unless that report is about whether the claimant is fit to be interviewed. An interview may establish protection needs without the need for medical evidence, and further supporting evidence can be submitted following the interview. For more information on considering medical reports in an asylum decision see guidance on medical evidence in asylum claims and the section on Particular interview needs. If the claimant is a child, you must refer to the guidance on Processing children’s asylum claims.

Appropriateness of interviewing by video conference (VC)

In some exceptional cases, conducting an interview via VC may not be appropriate, though this will depend on the circumstances of the individual case. When deciding whether to use VC you need to consider whether the claimant has any sight or hearing impairment, mental health issues, learning disabilities or difficulties, or if there are other factors that may prevent a claimant disclosing particularly sensitive information in a VC interview and, in the case of children, whether the use of VC is in accordance with the duty under section 55. For further information on the appropriateness of using VC when interviewing children see Processing children’s asylum claims guidance.

This does not mean that VC will not be appropriate, but any reasons given by the claimant for not wanting an interview to be conducted by VC must be carefully considered. This may include, but is not limited to, cases involving sexual orientation or gender identity, victims of torture or other trauma where recording was part of the persecution, victims of sexual violence or other forms of gender-based persecution, victims of modern slavery or claimants with mental health conditions. A decision to continue with a VC interview despite a request to the contrary from the claimant should be fully justified and recorded in the claimant’s records.

Where you assess based on the evidence available that a VC interview is not appropriate, then you should inform the claimant that a face-to-face interview will be organised.

Alternatively, some claimants with specific needs may prefer remote interviews. These individual factors are something that you must take into consideration when deciding whether to use VC or interview in person.

Where it becomes clear during a VC interview that the claimant is unable to participate fully in the interview process, you must try to establish the reasons why and then take a break, seeking advice from a Senior Caseworker or Technical Specialist as necessary. If the interview cannot continue as a VC interview, it should be rearranged as a face-to-face interview.

In cases where the VC interview is suspended because the claimant is unable to participate fully in the interview process, and is rearranged as a face-to-face interview, decision-makers should take a case-by-case approach as to what point the face-to-face interview starts from. Decision-makers should consider recapping where the interview was suspended and signposting to what will be covered next. Claimants should not be obliged to recount their experience again if it is not entirely necessary.

Remote video conferencing pilot

Most asylum interviews take place by way of video conference, with the claimant located at a Home Office or Visas Facilitation Services (VFS) building.

The Home Office is piloting a new approach to interviewing adult asylum claimants by way of video conference, with the claimant located in their own accommodation or premises belonging to their immigration adviser. The aim of the pilot is to trial a process to increase the number of asylum interviews that can be conducted, and to help improve the claimant experience.

The Home Office recognises that this method of interviewing will not be appropriate for all claimants. For the purposes of the pilot, claimants who are considered to be a high harm risk or who are particularly vulnerable will not be invited to participate in the pilot. This includes, but is not limited to:

foreign national offenders, or claimants with pending prosecutions for an offence which if convicted would make them a potential candidate for exclusion under Article 1(F) of the Refugee Convention or exclusion from a grant of humanitarian protection under paragraph 339D of the Immigration Rules, or refusal of refugee status under paragraph 334(iii) or 334(iv) of the Immigration Rules

potential and confirmed victims of modern slavery or human trafficking where the exploitation is alleged to have occurred, or is accepted to the relevant standard of proof to have occurred in the UK

potential and confirmed victims of domestic abuse in the UK

those with safeguarding concerns relating to suicide and self-harm

Where a claimant is identified as being potentially suitable for the pilot, the Home Office may write to the claimant and where relevant, their immigration adviser to enquire whether they are willing and able to participate in the pilot. This correspondence must describe the interview process and the requirements, for example, that the claimant must have access to the necessary IT equipment and a confidential space in which to conduct the interview (for example, a quiet room in their own accommodation). It must also explain that participation in the pilot is entirely voluntary and if the claimant does not want to participate or cannot participate because they do not have the means to do so, it will not have any negative impact on the consideration of their asylum claim.

Where a claimant does not want to participate in the pilot or cannot participate because they do not have the means to do so (for example, they do not have the necessary IT equipment), their asylum claim will continue to be considered as normal. They may therefore be invited to attend an interview at a Home Office or VFS building.

Interviewing officers must continue to apply all relevant aspects of the guidance on asylum interviews when conducting interviews as part of the remote video conferencing pilot. This includes guidance on safeguarding.

This section provides interviewing officers with additional guidance on how to conduct an asylum interview as part of the remote video conferencing interview pilot.

Video connection

You must not begin the interview unless the claimant’s video camera is switched on, and you can clearly see the claimant. The claimant’s video camera must also be of sufficient quality to enable you to verify their identity as set out in the section on Verifying Identity.

If the claimant’s video camera does not work, or for any other reason a clear and stable video connection to the claimant cannot be established, you must suspend the interview. The interview must then be rescheduled to take place at a Home Office or VFS location.

The claimant must remain on camera and be clearly visible to you throughout the duration of the interview. If video connection is lost at any point, for any reason, the interview must be immediately paused and not resumed unless clear video connection is re-established. If video connection to the claimant cannot be re-established, the interview must be suspended and rescheduled to take place at a Home Office or VFS location.

Confidentiality

For reasons of confidentiality, you must normally interview the claimant alone or in the presence of their immigration adviser. In exceptional circumstances, claimants may also be interviewed in the presence of a friend or other companion. For further information on the circumstances in which a friend or companion may be permitted to be present during an asylum interview refer to Friends, companions or supporters.

Claimants are informed ahead of the interview that they will be required to show their interview environment to the interviewing officer. Claimants are therefore also informed that they must access the video conference interview with a device that is capable of being rotated to provide a 360-degree view of their interview environment.

Before starting the interview, you must ask the claimant to provide you with a 360-degree view of their interview environment using their video camera. This typically involves asking the claimant to rotate their device in a way that ensures you have seen each corner of the room that they are in, but a claimant may be given further instructions depending on their interview environment. The purpose of this is to verify that no unauthorised materials, devices, or people are present, ensuring that the integrity of the asylum interview is upheld.

You must also ask the claimant to provide you with a 360-degree view of their interview environment in the following circumstances:

after a break, before resuming the interview

after a temporary loss in video connection, no matter the duration

at a random point during the interview

At the start of the interview, you must explain to the claimant that you will ask them to show you their interview environment at a random point during the interview.

Where a claimant is not able to provide you with a full view of their interview environment, for example, because they are using a static device such as a desktop to conduct the interview, you must cancel the interview. The interview must be rescheduled to take place at a Home Office or VFS building.

If at any point you have cause to suggest that the claimant’s interview environment is not confidential, you must immediately suspend the interview. This may occur, for example, where there are unauthorised third parties present, you can hear but cannot see other people talking in the background, you have reason to believe that unauthorised parties can overhear what is being discussed in the interview, or where the claimant is in a public space. These examples are not exhaustive. Where an interview is cancelled or suspended due to concerns over confidentiality, it must be rescheduled to take place at a Home Office or VFS building.

We will keep the pilot under review.

When a child turns 18 before the asylum interview

If an asylum seeker makes a claim as a child, but their 18th birthday passes before an asylum interview has been conducted, they are legally an adult. An asylum seeker who has recently turned 18 is a young adult and as their asylum claim relates to circumstances experienced as a child, you must take into account their age, level of maturity and experiences when interviewing and deciding the claim. For further details about how to handle these cases, refer to the guidance on Processing children’s asylum claims. The claimant should be interviewed by a decision maker who is trained to deal with asylum claims from children. The claimant must also be given an opportunity to discuss the statement of evidence form (SEF) as it may refer to issues that are child specific.

Dependants, children and families

You must follow the asylum instruction on Dependants and former dependants and Family Asylum Claims which provides the policy and procedures for considering an asylum claim which also includes the main claimant’s partner and or children under the age of 18.

In cases where a child’s asylum claim is being considered as part of a Family Asylum Claim you should normally expect the principal claimant to set out protection needs on behalf of their children, and this should avoid putting children through an interview process unnecessarily. However, you have discretion to interview any dependant or claimant, subject to age and maturity, where it is appropriate and relevant to do so. This can include, but is not limited to, cases where:

evidence has been submitted prior to the interview of the principal claimant which indicates interviewing a dependant or claimant will assist in making an informed decision on the claim

evidence arises during the interview of the principal claimant which requires further investigation to make an informed decision

To conduct an asylum interview with a claimant under 18 years of age you must be trained to interview children in line with the standards and procedures set out in the guidance on Processing children’s asylum claims.

Even if a separate interview is not considered necessary, you must not lose sight of the child as an individual, as well as part of a family during the interview process. You must be vigilant and responsive to their protection and welfare needs and consider how this could impact on the needs of the whole family. You must also be aware that child protection issues may arise in the context of the family unit.

Where a decision is made to interview a dependant, a separate invitation to interview must be issued to that dependant. The dependant may wish to obtain legal advice and arrange for an immigration adviser or, in the case of a child, a responsible adult, to attend the interview. Where an immigration adviser has already been instructed, they must be informed in advance about any proposed interviews of dependants.

Pregnancy and maternity

Claimants who are pregnant are not expected to attend an asylum interview in the 6-week period leading up to their due date.

You can ask expectant claimants to attend an interview until around 6 weeks before the due date for the birth, unless they have been advised not to attend on medical grounds. Any advice not to attend an interview must be supported by a letter from the GP or consultant, or other appropriately qualified healthcare professional involved in their maternity care, such as a midwife, nurse or health visitor, regulated by the:

General Medical Council (GMC)

Health & Care Professions Council (HCPC)

Nursing & Midwifery Council (NMC)

For claimants who have given birth, you must not normally arrange interviews until at least 6 weeks after the birth. Where a claimant’s individual circumstances means that it would be unreasonable to expect them to attend an asylum interview, for example, due to pregnancy complications, or because they would have to travel far to attend to interview, you are able to use discretion and flexibility on the 6-week timeframe to attend an interview before or after birth. You should consult with the claimant or immigration advisers and if there are health concerns for the mother or baby, you should postpone the interview until they are well enough and obtain medical evidence from one of the bodies or individuals listed above to support any further delay. You should also consider Paragraphs 339NA of the Immigration Rules and whether any of the circumstances in which an interview may be omitted apply, to prevent any further delay.

There may be cases where a claimant is interviewed after giving birth to a child who is not a British citizen, and at the time of the interview, their child is not treated as a dependant on their asylum claim, nor is the child an asylum claimant in their own right. Where this is the case, you must explain to the claimant that if they want to include their child as a dependant on their asylum claim, they must attend an in-person appointment together with their child so that the child can be registered as a dependant on their asylum claim or if their child has protection needs, as an asylum claimant. After the interview, you must send the claimant correspondence explaining how to schedule an appointment to register their child as a dependant or asylum claimant in person at a screening location. For further information, see the guidance on Dependants and former dependants.

Childcare during asylum interviews

You must not expect parents to give an account of past persecution in front of their children. This is to protect the claimant’s own interests and those of the child, bearing in mind the statutory duty to safeguard and promote the welfare of children. Parents may be reluctant to reveal difficult information with a child present, it may be traumatising for the claimant, or the child and the parent may be distracted whilst trying to look after a child and provide evidence.

Childcare is not available at the interview sites. Interviews of single parents should generally be scheduled when school-age children are attending school. Claimants who are invited to interview who have young children that require childcare and who are unable to make alternative care arrangements, should contact the Home Office using the contact details provided on the invitation to interview to reschedule their interview or seek alternative ways for information to be gathered, for example, by providing a witness statement, questionnaire, or other documentary evidence.

Where no other childcare is available, there may be exceptional circumstances where babies may be present in the room whilst the interview is taking place. For example, the parent would prefer to be present with the child (for example, due to the need to breastfeed), the child is younger than 12 months old, will not be able to understand the content of the interview, and is not distracting to the claimant (for example, because they are napping). If you are unsure, you must seek advice from a Technical Specialist or Senior Caseworker. You must also ensure that you take breaks as appropriate and ensure the wellbeing of everyone in the room.

Whether an interview can proceed in the presence of a baby will depend on the circumstances. In all cases, you must ensure that you are able to conduct a fair and effective asylum interview which will enable the claimant to put forward all relevant information in their case without distraction.

Non-attendance

You must normally require all asylum claimants to attend an interview, except where it may be omitted in accordance with paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules. In circumstances where Paragraph 339NA does not apply, the interview will be rescheduled as soon as possible in cases where a claimant provides evidence that they were unable to attend for circumstances beyond their control. It may be appropriate in some circumstances to omit the interview where a claimant is unfit to attend an interview, and it is not possible to reschedule this should be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

Omitting the asylum interview

An interview may be omitted (see paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules) where:

you are able to make a decision to grant asylum or humanitarian protection without it

the Home Office has already met with the applicant for the purpose of assisting them with completing their application and submitting the essential information regarding their application

the applicant has only raised issues that are not relevant or of minimal relevance to the examination of whether they are a refugee / eligible for humanitarian protection

the applicant has made inconsistent, contradictory, improbable or insufficient representations which make their claim clearly unconvincing in relation to having been the object of persecution or serious harm

the applicant has submitted a subsequent application which does not raise any relevant new elements with respect to their particular circumstances or to the situation in their country of origin

the applicant is making an application merely in order to delay or frustrate the enforcement of an earlier or imminent decision which would result in their removal

you are of the opinion that it is not reasonably practicable to do so, for example because the applicant is unfit or unable to be interviewed owing to enduring circumstances beyond their control

the applicant is an EU national (whose claim has been determined to be unsuitable for inadmissibility action and instead will be considered substantively)

Non-attendance due to illness

If the claimant is unable to attend or proceed with an interview due to illness or a medical condition, the claimant or their immigration adviser must generally provide a letter or certificate, or another appropriate form of evidence. The evidence must be from a GP, consultant or other appropriately qualified relevant healthcare professional regulated by one of the following regulators:

General Medical Council (GMC)

Health & Care Professions Council (HCPC)

Nursing & Midwifery Council (NMC)

General Dental Council (GDC)

Whilst there may be genuine reasons why an individual is unable to attend an interview. All claimants must inform the Home Office ahead of time if they are unable to attend. It is not considered reasonable for claimants to continually delay or avoid attending their asylum interview. The interview is an important opportunity to provide information about the reasons someone is seeking protection. Refer to the Withdrawing asylum claims guidance for the timescales claimants have to provide reasons and evidence for their non-attendance.

On receipt of any medical evidence, you must check that it has been compiled by a suitably qualified, relevant, healthcare professional regulated by the GMC, HCPC, NMC or GDC, and consider the evidence to establish when you can rebook the interview or consider whether the interview can be omitted in line with paragraph 339NA of the Immigration Rules.

If the claimant is detained, it is expected that the interview will be conducted while they are in detention. As with non-detained cases, claimants in detention who do not attend an interview due to medical reasons are expected to provide evidence to support them being unable to attend or proceed with an interview. This is to enable the interview to be rearranged, and the asylum claim processed as quickly as possible. The Withdrawing asylum claims guidance provides detailed instructions on how much time a detained claimant has to provide reasons and evidence for their non-attendance or inability to complete an interview.

Where a claimant is detained, their particular circumstances and continued eligibility for detention must be considered in line with the detained asylum process policy with reference to the adults at risk policy and detention criteria and Rule 35 processes. However, claimants must not normally be released for the sole reason of waiting for medical evidence about their suitability to attend an interview. For more information refer to the Asylum Policy Instruction on medical evidence in asylum claims.

You should consider any explanation provided, for example, they were admitted to hospital and, if accepted as a circumstance beyond their control, you can rebook the interview. If no explanation is provided, or you do not consider the explanation to be satisfactory, you may treat the claim as withdrawn. See the Withdrawing asylum claims guidance.

If the evidence shows that the claimant is mentally or physically unable, for the foreseeable future, to cope with an interview you must consult a Senior Caseworker, taking into account the requirements of Paragraph 339NA(vii) of the Immigration Rules. You will need to discuss whether there are alternative methods to gather information and evidence regarding their asylum claim, for example through provision of a witness statement, questionnaire or through documentary evidence where available. See also mental illness.

If the claimant states that they are unwell or you observe that they are unwell at the beginning of or during an interview, you should establish the severity of the situation. In a more severe situation, your focus will shift to meeting the claimant’s immediate health needs which may involve taking safeguarding action or calling an ambulance. In a less severe situation, you may be able to establish the following:

why they feel unwell

whether they feel able or unable to proceed with the interview

whether they have seen a medical professional about any condition, and can provide evidence of this appointment and the outcome, including any diagnosis, as soon as practicable within the 7 days

when their condition started and whether they have any diagnosis or prognosis from a clinician

what, if any, medication they have been prescribed and are taking

how the condition impacts on day-to-day living and how it is affecting them during the interview

if the claimant is detained, whether they sought, or tried to obtain, evidence with an emphasis on their suitability to be interviewed in detention prior to the interview

if the condition is pre-existing and they didn’t try to obtain evidence on their suitability to be interviewed prior to the interview, why they did not do this

when they expect to be better and able to proceed with the interview

if they wish to stop the interview, under what conditions they think they will be able to proceed, for example once they have taken medication or seen a GP

whether there is anything you could do to enable the interview to proceed, including referring the claimant to an on-site nurse or other medical professional for a medical assessment

For further information see medical evidence in asylum claims.

You should explore with the claimant the implications of continuing or suspending the interview, considering both the need to protect the claimant’s health, and the possibility of delays to the process if the interview is suspended. This will include making the claimant aware that suspending an interview may delay a decision on their asylum claim or potentially mean a longer period in detention, depending on the particular facts of the case and the circumstances of the individual.

If after discussion, the claimant agrees to continue with the interview, you must offer breaks as appropriate. You must also regularly check how they are feeling and whether they still feel able to continue at key moments, for example, when resuming the interview after a break, or after an episode in which sensitive matters have been discussed.

If you decide that the claimant is not fit to be interviewed, you should cancel or suspend the interview with the claimant’s agreement. If the claimant insists on continuing you must consult with a HEO or SEO.

Once an interview is rebooked after a previous incidence of non-attendance, the subsequent invitation to interview must explain to the claimant that if they fail to attend their next scheduled interview appointment, their claim may be withdrawn if they fail to inform the Home Office that they cannot attend before or on the date of the interview. See Withdrawing asylum claims.

All requests or decisions to cancel or suspend an asylum interview due to sickness must be signed off by a HEO or SEO and all relevant details must be noted on Home Office records.

Non-attendance for other reasons

If the claimant states that they were unable to attend due to severe travel delays or disruption, they must explain and where necessary provide acceptable evidence of this, for example, information from the travel company or news reports of severe disruption. For wide-scale travel disruption known to the Home Office it may also be evident without the need to request specific evidence. You must consider whether any explanation for non-attendance is reasonable.

The Home Office may also cancel interviews in advance if they become aware ahead of time of widespread disruption (for example, national strikes). These interviews will be rescheduled as soon as possible.

You must not accept explanations such as the unavailability of the immigration adviser to meet with the claimant before the interview, unavailability of their immigration adviser or interpreter for the scheduled interview, attendance at college or, where permission to work has been granted, employment commitments.

Treat the claim as withdrawn because of non-attendance

If the claimant does not attend and no explanation is received within the timescales set out in the Withdrawing asylum claims guidance, or the response received does not evidence that they failed to attend due to circumstances beyond their control, or contact is lost and the immigration adviser is unable to assist, you should normally treat the claim as withdrawn and stop considering it, in line with paragraph 333C of the Immigration Rules. For further advice see guidance on withdrawing asylum claims.

Pending prosecutions

If a claimant is awaiting an interview and checks reveal there is a pending prosecution, Home Office staff will need to decide whether to proceed with an interview, or whether to immediately put the case on hold and delay interviewing until the outcome of the pending prosecution is known. In general, interviews should not normally be delayed while awaiting the outcome of a pending prosecution even if the subsequent asylum decision will need to be paused to await the prosecution outcome.

If you believe there is a reason why the interview should be delayed, you must discuss this with your SCW and obtain agreement to put the case on hold. This is because, even if the case is subsequently paused at the decision-making stage, it is important that processing can resume as soon as the outcome of the pending prosecution is known. Further information is available in the Pending prosecutions in asylum claims guidance.

Choice of language

Asylum interviews must be conducted in a language that the claimant can communicate in to a sufficient level for the purpose of the asylum interview.

Before inviting the claimant to attend an asylum interview, you must review all available evidence to determine the language that the interview should be conducted in.

A claimant may have been screened in one language but expressed a preference for the asylum interview to be conducted in another language.

If you cannot find an interpreter in their preferred language, you may use an interpreter who speaks the language used at the screening interview or another language it is considered there is evidence that the claimant is proficient in. Various factors may demonstrate or indicate proficiency in another language (including English), including where the claimant:

completed a visa application in English

completed a visa application interview in English

entered the UK on an immigration route which required demonstrating proficiency in English

completed a Screening Interview in English

submitted documentation in English

spent time in education in another country where that language was utilised

undertaken a job role in another country where that language was utilised

spent time in the UK to become further accustomed to the English language

requested permission to work whilst an asylum claim is pending in the UK

You must explain this to the claimant and conduct the interview in the language used at the screening interview or the language it is considered the claimant is proficient in, unless the claimant’s command of the language is not good enough for the asylum interview.

Where attempts are made to interview the claimant in another language and it is clear the claimant and interpreter do not understand each other, you should suspend the interview. You should review the case and contact a SCW for advice if necessary. See also languages at interview.

There may be cases where a claimant attends their asylum interview but refuses to complete the interview because we have been unable to source an interpreter in their preferred language. If it is considered that the claimant’s command of another language is good enough to conduct an asylum interview, you must expect the claimant to continue with the interview as arranged. Where the claimant refuses to complete the interview, you must warn them that their asylum claim may be decided based on available evidence, which may result in their asylum claim being refused due to non-compliance under paragraph 339M of the Immigration Rules. Once you have issued this warning, you must give the claimant an opportunity to speak to their immigration adviser if they have one. Where the claimant still refuses to complete the interview, you must suspend the interview. The interview record must include details of the reason why the interview has been suspended and must record any warnings issued to the claimant prior to the suspension.

Requests for a male or female interviewer or interpreter

Claimants are asked at the screening interview if they would like a male or female interviewer (and where applicable interpreter). They are also asked again in the invitation to interview and advised to contact us if they have a preference and have not advised us already and that we will do our best to arrange this.

When a request for a male or female interviewer or interpreter is made in advance of the interview, you should make every effort to meet this requirement as far as operationally possible. This includes making any requests for a gender specific interpreter clear to the Interpreter & Language Services Unit (ILSU) booking team, by completing the comments section of the booking request. If a claimant’s request cannot be met on the scheduled day, the interview should normally be rearranged.

If a claimant states a preference for a male or female interviewer or interpreter for the first time on the actual day of the interview, you must consider whether this can be accommodated. If it can’t be accommodated, you must proceed with the interview as planned unless there are any vulnerabilities or other reasons that come to light that suggest the interview should be rearranged. The decision to proceed with, or to rearrange, an interview must be agreed with a Senior Caseworker and noted on Home Office records.

In all cases, you must also be aware of gender related issues, since this may affect how the claimant responds during the interview. See:

Gender issues in the asylum claim

Gender identity issues in the asylum claim

Sexual orientation issues in the asylum claim

Friends, companions or supporters

For reasons of confidentiality, you will normally interview a claimant on their own or in the presence of a immigration adviser, regulated adviser, or professional support worker from a Non-Governmental-Organisation (NGO). Exceptionally, however, and with advance notice, you may allow a friend or other companion of the claimant to be present to provide emotional or medical support. For example, if an interviewer of the requested gender has not been possible. Alternatively, a claimant may benefit from the presence of a supporter from their faith group or non-religious organisation before or during the interview, and this can also be accommodated exceptionally and where advance notice is provided.

However, you must keep in mind the need to safeguard against the possibility that a trafficker or smuggler may use this as an opportunity to influence or monitor the claimant’s asylum claim. You must therefore first establish with the claimant alone whether they are content for the friend, companion or supporter to be present during the interview. The interviewer must also consider whether the claimant might be under the control of a trafficker. If it is a known or suspected trafficking case, the identity of the friend, companion or supporter must be carefully considered before the interview can proceed or continue if suspicion is raised during the interview itself. You may also ask for ID documents in order to ascertain the identity of the person accompanying the claimant.

A friend, companion or supporter must not be permitted to attend if they:

are a family member

are seeking asylum separately themselves

have any obvious personal interest in the outcome of the claim

have engaged in providing legal advice to the claimant

Whilst it is important to keep the presence of a friend, companion, or supporter to a minimum, you must discuss any request from the claimant with a Senior Caseworker and accommodate this if there are exceptional circumstances which would mean that this is appropriate.

A friend, companion or supporter can be admitted on condition that they are there solely to provide emotional, medical, or spiritual support. They must not intervene during the interview unless it is to raise a welfare or safeguarding concern with the claimant, using the Home Office interpreter. You must observe and record this interaction and then complete your own welfare check. A friend, companion or supporter must observe complete confidentiality afterwards. You must explain this to the claimant as well as any friend, companion, or supporter, so that they are fully aware of what is expected. If you become concerned about the behaviour, conduct or interventions of the friend, companion or supporter during the interview, you must consider whether it is appropriate to ask them to leave or suspend the interview. This may involve speaking to the claimant separately or discussing the case with a senior manager, depending on the circumstances.

Religious festivals

You must be sensitive and respectful of any religious beliefs and practices. However, asylum is an important matter, and you must normally require claimants to attend an interview even if the date coincides with a religious festival or a period of fasting. You must also consider whether any reasonable adjustments are appropriate, for example, if a claimant is fasting. For reference purposes, the interfaith calendar provides the relevant dates for religious festivals. Further information on religions and faiths can be found at the inter-faith network for the United Kingdom.

Health, safety and risk assessments

You must check the file, database notes and any special conditions in advance of the interview, in case of any known risk factors relating to the claimant, such as previous verbal or physical abuse, threats to commit suicide or self-harm or criminal convictions. You must inform security and management if there is reason to believe that a claimant could be a danger to the safety of themselves, interpreters, other claimants or staff, so that they can take steps to manage any risk. Risk factors may also be relevant to assessing whether an interview is in-person or remote and whether it is reasonably practicable to interview the claimant in accordance with paragraph 339NA(vii) of the Immigration Rules.

Where there is cause to suggest that a claimant may be a danger to themselves or others and it is still considered appropriate to interview the claimant, the claimant must be invited to attend an interview at a Home Office building. Security and management staff at the interview location must be aware so that appropriate safeguards can be put in place.

Interviews in prison

You must contact the prison to arrange a time and date for the interview and, once arranged, serve notice of the interview on the claimant.
